title: Laser Shots
statement: Painted panels hang along a wall, and each panel covers a closed span [left, right] of integer positions. A laser fired straight at integer position x marks every panel whose span contains x, meaning left <= x <= right. Spans may overlap, touch, be nested or repeat. Return the fewest shots needed so that every panel is marked at least once. A shot may be fired at any integer position, including one outside the listed spans.

examples.explanation: A shot at 2 marks [0, 2] and [-3, 4]; a shot at 10 marks [3, 10] and [9, 15]; [14, 16] needs its own shot at 16. The spans [0, 2], [3, 10] and [14, 16] are pairwise disjoint, so three shots are unavoidable.
The spans are pairwise disjoint, so no position lies in two of them and each needs its own shot.

hints.content: Look at the panel whose right end is smallest. Some shot has to land somewhere inside that panel.
Every other panel ends at or after this panel's right end. So any panel marked by an earlier position inside it is also marked by its right end.
That means the right end is never worse than any other position for this panel: fire there.
Sort the panels by right end. Fire at the right end of the first panel that is not yet marked.
Keep lastShot. A panel is already marked when left <= lastShot (spans are closed); otherwise fire at its right end and update lastShot. Sorting dominates the running time.

testCases.explanation: Overlapping spans with one nested inside another.
Four pairwise disjoint spans, one of them a single point.
Spans are closed, so all three contain position 7 and one shot marks them.
Nested spans: a shot at 0 marks the three nested spans, and [2, 4] needs a second shot.
Identical single-point spans share one shot.
Extreme coordinates: shots at -1000000 and 1000000 mark all three.
One long span with four disjoint spans inside it needs four shots.
Large input of short clusters laid out along the wall.
Large input of random spans over the full coordinate range.

solutions.title: Try every set of shot positions, smallest sets first
solutions.intuition: Only the set of shots matters, so try every set of candidate positions in increasing size and stop at the first one that marks every panel.
solutions.approach: A shot can always be slid to the nearest panel endpoint without losing a panel, so the candidate positions are the distinct left and right ends of the panels. For k = 0, 1, 2, ... enumerate every k-element subset of the candidates; the first k for which some subset marks every panel (left <= x <= right for a chosen x) is the answer.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(C(m, k) * n * k) for m distinct endpoints, n panels and an answer of k shots, which is exponential in the number of panels
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(m) for the candidate list and the recursion over at most k chosen positions
commonMistakes: Testing open spans (left < x < right), which wrongly separates panels that merely touch at an endpoint.
Returning the first subset that marks every panel without trying smaller sizes first, which can report more shots than necessary.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This is the definition: try every set of shot positions in increasing size and report the first size that works. Sliding a shot onto the nearest panel endpoint never loses a panel, so only endpoints need to be tried, but the number of subsets still grows exponentially with the number of distinct endpoints. It is a correctness oracle for a handful of panels, not a solution for thousands.

steps.title: Collect the candidates
steps.content: The first example has ten distinct endpoints: -3, 4, 0, 2, 3, 10, 9, 15, 14 and 16.

steps.title: Grow the set size
steps.content: No set of zero, one or two positions marks all five panels (the panels [0, 2], [3, 10] and [14, 16] are pairwise disjoint). Some set of three, for example {2, 10, 16}, does, so the answer is 3.

solutions.title: Quadratic DP for the largest set of pairwise disjoint panels
solutions.intuition: A shot marks only panels that contain its position, so two disjoint panels can never share a shot. The answer is therefore at least the size of the largest set of pairwise disjoint panels, and that size is exactly the answer.
solutions.approach: Sort the panels by right end. Let chain[i] be the most pairwise disjoint panels in a chain ending with panel i: 1 plus the best chain[j] over earlier panels j that end before panel i starts. The largest chain is the answer. It is a lower bound because disjoint panels need separate shots, and it is reachable because the greedy strategy never fires more shots than the largest disjoint set.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n^2) after the O(n log n) sort
commonMistakes: Treating touching spans as disjoint; closed spans that share an endpoint share a shot, so the chain test must be right[j] < left[i], not <=.
Sorting by left end, which breaks the order the DP relies on.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Panels that are pairwise disjoint need separate shots, so the answer is at least the size of the largest disjoint set, which this DP computes in O(n^2). The bound is tight. The greedy strategy fires only when a panel starts after the previous shot, and the panels that trigger shots are pairwise disjoint (each starts after the shot fired at the previous trigger's right end). So greedy uses at most as many shots as the largest disjoint set, and no strategy can use fewer, which means the DP and the greedy always agree. The greedy simply skips the quadratic work.

steps.title: Build chains
steps.content: chain = 1, 1, 2, 2, 3: [14, 16] starts after [3, 10] ends, which in turn starts after [0, 2] ends. The largest chain is 3.

solutions.title: Sort by right end and shoot greedily
solutions.intuition: Firing at the smallest right end among unmarked panels marks the most panels any choice for that panel could.
solutions.approach: Copy and sort the panels by right end. Walk them, keeping the last shot position. A panel with left > lastShot is unmarked: count a shot and fire at its right end.
solutions.pseudocode:
sort panels by right end
shots = 0; lastShot = -infinity
for (l, r) in panels: if l > lastShot: shots += 1; lastShot = r
return shots
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the sort, then O(n)
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sorted copy of the panels
commonMistakes: Sorting by left end and shooting at the smallest right end seen so far, which needs extra bookkeeping.
Using left >= lastShot, which fires a needless extra shot for touching spans.
Sorting the caller's array in place and mutating the input.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Take the panel with the smallest right end r. Some shot must hit it, and every other panel ends at or after r, so a panel that contains any shot inside this one also contains r. Firing at r is therefore never worse, so an exchange argument shows the greedy choice is safe. After firing, all panels with left <= r are marked; the rest are handled the same way. Sorting by right end is O(n log n), the scan is O(n), and the sorted copy costs O(n) memory (O(1) if sorting the input in place is allowed).

steps.title: First shot
steps.content: left 0 > -infinity so fire at 2; [-3, 4] has left -3 <= 2 and is marked.

steps.title: Second and third shots
steps.content: [3, 10] has left 3 > 2, so fire at 10; [9, 15] is marked. [14, 16] has left 14 > 10, so fire at 16. Three shots.
